title: Sexual assault survivors’ stories may shift over time – a psychologist explains why it doesn’t mean they’re lying
url:
<title>Sexual assault survivors’ stories may shift over time – a psychologist explains why it doesn’t mean they’re lying</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765035/original/file-20261008-50-3ru69c.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C3000%2C2000&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A majority of rape survivors don&#39;t immediately recognize what they experienced as rape. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/student-walks-past-a-sign-condemning-the-cornell-university-news-photo/2298596106">Ryan Murphy/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>If a person’s story changes in the weeks following an alleged sexual assault, are they not telling the truth?</p>

<p>It’s a criticism I’ve seen on social media and heard in the public conversation surrounding the <a href="https://www.courthousenews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/doe-cornell-new-york-supreme.pdf">lawsuit filed in September 2026</a> by a plaintiff known as Jane Doe, a former student at Cornell University, accusing seven male students of rape.  </p>

<p>Initially, Doe discussed events with her friend a friend but <a href="https://www.cbsnews.com/news/jane-doe-cornell-university-rape-allegations-text-messages-transcripts/">reportedly didn’t identify them as assault</a>. It wasn’t until weeks later, when her experience was labeled as a gang rape by others, that <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/01/nyregion/cornell-rape-accusation-reporting.html">she came forward to authorities</a>.</p>

<p>Survivors are often questioned about <a href="https://theconversation.com/traumatic-memories-are-often-fragmented-a-psychologist-explains-how-and-why-that-happens-284536">how they relay their stories</a>. When societal expectations about how rape survivors should respond do not align with the victim’s experience, it’s easy to assume that the victim is lying and the assailant is innocent.</p>

<p>Research indicates 60% to 70% of female rape survivors <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/1524838015576391">do not identify their experience as rape</a>. That’s especially true for college students. Instead, rape survivors often describe their experience in more general terms, referring to it as <a href="https://doi.org/10.1037/tra0002083">“bad sex” or “miscommunication.”</a> That’s both because of how sexual assault affects a survivor’s mind, brain and body and because of how society thinks about rape.</p>

<p>In my experience <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=vHIbLycAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">as a psychologist</a> doing crisis intervention work with rape and sexual assault victims, it is very common for survivors to prefer to continue as if the assault never happened and to be driven by a strong desire to return to normalcy.  While this seems counterintuitive, understanding the biological and psychological survival processes that sexual assault can activate may help explain why this response is perfectly logical.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/8cEiDrwkjwo?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">The sexual assault allegations against the so-called Cornell 7 have spurred national outrage.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Trauma’s immediate impact</h2>

<p>Immediately following a rape, survivors – whether they characterize their experience as rape or not – often experience myriad symptoms broadly referred to as <a href="https://doi.org/10.1176/ajp.131.9.981">rape trauma syndrome</a>. These symptoms include <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/bsl.2370010310">self-blame, emotional dysregulation</a> and feelings of fear and humiliation. These symptoms often lead to problems with sleep, headaches, muscle tension and fatigue.</p>

<p>Psychologists generally diagnose symptoms consistent with rape trauma syndrome as <a href="https://traumadissociation.com/acutestressdisorder">acute stress disorder</a>. Acute stress disorder reflects the unique psychological reactions immediately following trauma, whereas the longer-term effects are characterized as post-traumatic stress disorder, or PTSD.</p>

<p>People with acute stress disorder experience at least nine symptoms across several categories, including avoidance of trauma reminders, persistent negative mood and dissociation – defined as a disconnection between thoughts, feelings and bodily sensations. Other symptoms include intrusive experiences like nightmares or flashbacks, feeling like they are reexperiencing the trauma, constantly being on high alert and having overly intense emotional reactions to reminders of the traumatic event.  </p>

<h2>The brain on trauma</h2>

<p>During acute stress, the brain shifts into survival mode. </p>

<p>Two of the main bodily systems activated during this period are the <a href="https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/body/limbic-system">limbic system</a> and the <a href="https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/body/hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal-hpa-axis">hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis</a>. The limbic system controls emotions, memory and behavior. The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis controls how the body responds to stress by regulating hormones like cortisol.  </p>

<p>These systems mobilize the body’s key survival responses – <a href="https://rainn.org/mental-health-therapy-support-after-sexual-violence/fight-flight-freeze-and-fawn-understanding-survival-responses/">fight, flight, freeze and fawn</a>.</p>

<p>When the limbic system and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.psyneuen.2018.08.023">kick in following trauma</a>, the internal commotion that ensues takes over the brain’s ability to control thinking, planning and decision-making. This effectively prevents the brain from making accurate sense of what happened and from coping with the trauma in a healthy way. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765082/original/file-20261008-50-5rbaeh.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Abstract 3D red glowing brain with neural connections and energy particles on a dark background." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765082/original/file-20261008-50-5rbaeh.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765082/original/file-20261008-50-5rbaeh.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765082/original/file-20261008-50-5rbaeh.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765082/original/file-20261008-50-5rbaeh.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765082/original/file-20261008-50-5rbaeh.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765082/original/file-20261008-50-5rbaeh.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765082/original/file-20261008-50-5rbaeh.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Trauma kicks the brain into survival mode and mobilizes the body’s survival responses.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/abstract-3d-red-glowing-human-brain-with-neural-royalty-free-image/2283979074">Iana Kunitsa/Moment via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Self-blame and denial are protective</h2>

<p>For rape survivors, a common outcome of this neurobiological storm is <a href="https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph20156530">self-blame</a> – a tendency to hold themselves responsible for the events that led to the trauma. Generally, people believe they live in a world that feels safe and predictable, and they tend to adhere to the <a href="https://dictionary.apa.org/just-world-hypothesis">just world hypothesis</a>, which posits that good things happen to good people. To preserve the illusion of control, safety and predictability, survivors blame themselves in an effort to to restore order to a world that has been incredibly shaken by trauma.  </p>

<p>Rape survivors often experience <a href="https://dictionary.apa.org/hindsight-bias">hindsight bias</a> – the belief that they should have been able to predict or prevent an assault. This belief, which further reinforces self-blame, is fortified by a culture in which rape prevention programs tend to <a href="https://vawnet.org/sites/default/files/materials/files/2016-09/AR_RapePrevention.pdf">focus on women as opposed to men</a>, leading women to believe they alone are responsible for and can prevent rape.</p>

<p>Then there’s <a href="https://dictionary-apa-org.libdata2015.hilbert.edu/denial">denial, a defense mechanism</a> that can take the form of avoidance of or dissociation from the trauma. Because the reality of what has happened is overwhelming to the brain and psyche, denying or ignoring it provides a defense from the flood of emotion that follows trauma and helps reestablish a sense of stability. </p>

<p>Common <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1471-6402.1994.tb00296.x">rape stereotypes</a> – for example, that rape is mainly committed by strangers in a novel situation, not by acquaintances during everyday experiences – reinforce these feelings. In fact, statistics indicate that 80% to 90% of women are <a href="https://nsvrc.org/statistic/5866/">raped by someone they know</a>. </p>

<h2>Judging a changing story</h2>

<p>A person assessing the reactions of a rape and trauma survivor generally does so in a calm and collected frame of mind. Yet the actions they are judging were made under extreme duress – under mental and physical hurricane conditions, you could say.  </p>

<p>For a survivor of rape, an inability to clearly name the assault for what it was is a common outcome of the biological and psychological factors at play during acute stress. This denial functions to preserve their identity and sanity during acute stress, restore order to their world and help them make rational sense of what has happened to them. </p>

<p>Breaking through these self-preservation mechanisms often takes time – time that observers too often misinterpret as a false accounting of what actually happened.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293766/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

title: ‘Nothing About This Was Inevitable’
excerpt: The second floor of OpenAI’s old headquarters had a theme
body: The second floor of OpenAI’s old headquarters had a theme
Each room was named after one of the most important inventions in human history: “Clock,” “Fire,” and, of course, “AGI,” or artificial general intelligence
I saw this in the spring of 2024, when I was interviewing some of the company’s researchers about recent technical advances
At the time, ChatGPT was still making embarrassing arithmetic errors, and the notion that the bot would ever rival human intelligence was dubious
But here, in the renovated shell of a former mayonnaise factory in San Francisco, AGI’s arrival was predestined

This belief in AGI—a computer program with capabilities that rival or even exceed those of the human mind—is foundational to the mission of Google DeepMind, OpenAI, and Anthropic, three of the most influential AI companies in the world

And the pursuit of that milestone is the subject of The AGI Chronicles , a new book by the tech reporter and Atlantic contributing writer Kevin Roose, which he describes as his attempt to document the decade “when the human monopoly on advanced intelligence ended, and a new world was born.” Roose, a prominent and well-connected commenter on the AI boom, follows the internecine world of the frontier AI companies in remarkable, at times almost insular, detail

Based on interviews with more than 150 researchers, executives, investors, and policy makers close to the technology’s development, The AGI Chronicles traces crucial moments across DeepMind, OpenAI, and Anthropic from 2015 through early 2026 to figure out how we got to this very messy moment in AI , and who’s responsible for what happens next. [ Read: The singularity is not what it seems ] If you scan statements from executives such as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, there is a sense of fatalism about the rise of AI
In my conversation with Amodei last year, he likened developing AI to operating an out-of-control bus: It can’t be stopped or even slowed, but perhaps it can be steered

In an interview last month, Altman called AI “an inevitability.” According to this framing, AI executives are simply conductors, doing their best to provide guardrails for an era that’s careering our way, whether anyone likes it or not

Roose’s book prompted me to consider a question that is often neglected in the mile-a-minute news cycle: Are the leading AI companies simply heralding an inevitable evolution of this technology, as many of them claim, or are they directing that advancement? The answer will have tremendous bearing on how we assign responsibility for the world taking shape around us
The AGI Chronicles is of both minds on the topic

On the one hand, Roose is very explicit that he is archiving decisions made by a small group of people. “AGI was not inevitable,” he writes, but “invented, developed, and commercialized by a few hundred people.” On the other hand, sometimes the book reads like a natural history, describing a procession of events outside the control of any specific group of people, an almost geologic force sweeping the planet as “a new world was born.” He notes how, throughout the years, various companies and officials had yet to “wake up.” By 2024, he writes, “the idea of going back to the old world, to a time before all this, seemed more delusional than expecting the exponential to continue.” At times, Roose’s book echoes the loss of agency professed by AI executives
Of course, the inevitability of any one outcome is a self-serving fabrication

There is no prophecy that a handful of Silicon Valley companies dictating their own rules, running roughshod over copyright law and environmental regulations while mucking up once-reliable internet services with AI features nobody asked for, will operate largely unencumbered
Industries take shape through decisions made by individual actors and investors, the collective desire of the public, and the action or inaction of regulators
If you look to the late 1800s, for example, it would have seemed likely that electric cars would dominate the market in the following century
America’s best-selling car in 1897 was electric, and in the 1910s, Henry Ford was trying to develop an electric car with Thomas Edison

But a series of technological limitations and human decisions—including various financial missteps and harsh criticism from advocates of petrol-powered cars—changed the course of history, leaving a legacy that we’re reckoning with more than a century later
In the 1950s, it seemed as if nuclear reactors were destined to dot the nation and power the future
But a series of political campaigns and spectacular errors—the anti-nuclear movement, Three Mile Island, Chernobyl—crushed the nuclear age before it ever really started

Then there was the Space Age and supersonic flight—there are so many seemingly inevitable technological eras that never quite made it, not so much because of technology itself as because of political and economic choices
There are, similarly, so many corporate behemoths—Standard Oil, Kodak, Bear Stearns—that, because of regulation or complacency or fraud, unraveled

The inverse holds for many technologies and companies considered inevitable today: Different regulatory environments, international agreements, or priorities for Pentagon labs could have stopped the development of an open and global internet, smartphones, social media
When I recently called Roose to discuss his book and ask what he made of the industry’s frequently prophetic tone, he initially told me he believes that “nothing about this was inevitable

These were decisions made by people.” But he then said that he wanted to “complicate” that: “Once scaling the transformer worked, and once the scaling laws were documented,” Roose said, “I think it was inevitable that the companies building this stuff would push it as far as they possibly could.” I’d like to further complicate that view
Beyond the urge to test the bounds of any technology and reap enormous profits, the industry has been shaped by very human decisions
AI researchers chose to train their models on troves of copyrighted works without seeking permission, leading to countless creators suddenly getting left out of the economic equation
OpenAI chose to rush a free-to-use ChatGPT to the market in late 2022, kicking off a hype cycle and a subsequent investment bonanza
Venture-capital, private-equity, and tech firms chose to sink untold billions into a still-unprofitable technology
Data-center developers chose to eschew solar panels in favor of combustion turbines, which they perceive as faster and more reliable
On the government side, Donald Trump has chosen to ignore or eliminate any substantive federal regulation of AI
An industry that negotiated royalty payments, prioritized clean energy, gave itself longer development cycles, or faced serious federal regulation might look entirely different
The question of inevitability and responsibility may sound arcane, but it has real ramifications

In the Bay Area, tied up with the myth of AI’s inevitability is a sort of spiritual devotion: “Thank you to the machines, and the structure of reality, for letting us understand a little more,” Altman wrote on X this week
The more you treat AI as inevitable, the more it seems like a cosmic force rather than a product resulting from industrial and commercial design choices
The more you treat AI as inevitable, the less you can hold any company or person responsible for things going wrong
The executives, in this view, are only fractionally more empowered than us in deciding what happens next; more important, everyone else needs to wake up

As Altman put it to Politico earlier this month, “The world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology.” In the months since Roose concluded his reporting, the AI industry and its products have risen to still-greater global prominence and triggered even greater fears

When I asked him what new chapters he might add if he were still writing, Roose said that he would end the book with the recent White House press conference in which Trump, Amodei, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, Elon Musk, and several other tech executives addressed AI-safety concerns

body: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture
Kimberly Guilfoyle was so close to getting it right
The Trump hanger-on—former fiancée to Don Jr. and the current ambassador to Greece—was exchanging messages with a man named Eric Deters, according to a bombshell Wall Street Journal story last night

Deters, a right-wing podcast host, failed political candidate, and suspended lawyer in Kentucky, wanted help in clearing up some tax issues, and also wanted the Trump administration to extradite a doctor whose alleged fraud victims he was advising in a legal case
Guilfoyle, the messages indicate, wanted money—in one instance, a $100,000 wire—and she wanted it untraceable
Guilfoyle was right to worry about secrecy
She was about to begin confirmation hearings for her ambassadorship, and understood the pay-to-play could hurt her

Yet neither she nor Deters could stop breaking the Stringer Bell rule by recording their skullduggery in writing. “It won’t show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express,” Guilfoyle wrote. “Please.” And in another: “Honey please I need you to get this done for me today.” Yet even as she laid these instructions out, she kept haranguing Deters for indiscretion. “I really wish you would stop papering all these things
It’s really dangerous and not helpful to you or me while you could simply just call me on signal,” she wrote, referring to the encrypted messaging app

In one message, she wrote, “If you write an email or a text about, l’m gonna kill you cause I love you but you’re so out of control.” Unfortunately for Guilfoyle, her Signal messages were not as safe a space as she might have wished. (The Journal does not reveal how it viewed the messages
Guilfoyle’s lawyer broadly disputed their authenticity to the paper but offered no details.) Somehow, this is not the only Trump scandal with Balkan ties in the news this week

The New York Times reported that James Blair and Chris LaCivita, who are ostensibly President Trump’s top political advisers, traveled—during an intense midterm campaign in which Republicans appear to be on the verge of serious setbacks—to advise a candidate in Bosnia and Herzegovina’s self-governing Serbian entity
Both of these stories show the way that many people in Trump’s orbit view their positions not as public service but as a profit center

There’s a long and often depressing pattern of former officials capitalizing on government and political work, but Trump’s aides aren’t even willing to wait until they take their leave to start taking
Trump world is a team of mercenaries, in some cases literally
Jared Kushner, who was a senior adviser in his first presidency and is married to his daughter Ivanka, continues to work as an envoy for Trump while pursuing business deals around the world

As Dexter Filkins wrote in The New Yorker in September, Kushner’s record as a diplomat is underwhelming, yet his financial gains have been enormous. “He represents a new kind of Washington figure, for whom public office serves as a means to extraordinary wealth,” Filkins wrote
Kushner and Ivanka Trump even have their own Balkan boondoggle, an attempt to develop an island in Albania that has run into legal and political difficulties

Earlier this year, the Times reported that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick helped negotiate access to Kazakh tungsten reserves for an American mining company, and the federal government provided $1.6 billion in financing
Lutnick’s sons and Trump’s sons are both involved with companies that stand to profit from the deal (though representatives for them have said that they did not play a role in the deal)

A Washington Post investigation this summer noted that Trump’s sons have invested heavily in defense-technology companies; the companies have scored “at least $3.2 billion in direct government business since the sons invested and an additional $3.1 billion in future contract options.” (Company representatives told the Post that they secured their business without assistance from Trump’s sons.) Where do any of these people get the idea that this is appropriate or that they can get away with it? From the president himself, naturally

Trump has moved on from small-scale grifts such as charging the Secret Service exorbitant fees to stay in his hotels during his first term to far more ambitious and lucrative schemes such as crypto ventures ; even conservative estimates put his gains during this term alone in the billions
Though Trump doesn’t have ethical scruples, he does have a sense of right and wrong: It’s right for him to profiteer, but wrong for others to make too much money from his name
That’s where Blair, LaCivita, and Guilfoyle may run into trouble
Politico reports that Republicans’ “knives are now fully out” for the two consultants

Trump himself weighed in on Truth Social , saying he was unaware of their clients but adding that he “will, on reflection, ask them and, if there’s a conflict, I will terminate them, immediately!” Firing them just before the midterms seems risky, as it might just create more chaos for Republicans, but they could make for good scapegoats after the fact

Trump has not spoken publicly about the Guilfoyle story, although Vice President Vance said he didn’t “ love that .” In a further embarrassment, the article emerged while Secretary of State Marco Rubio was visiting Athens

Perhaps inevitably, Guilfoyle’s relationship with Deters ended acrimoniously. “I have paid you $300,000 over the years,” he wrote her in 2025, adding, in an amusingly self-negating flourish, “As of this memo, I have not received one favor
I am not naive or a sucker.” She was not happy, either. “What a nightmare you’ll literally cost me my ambassadorship stop writing,” she told him at one point, per the Journal
Related: MAGA is making the world safe for corruption
The watchdogs are barking themselves hoarse

The new charge has been added to the federal case against the couple, who are scheduled for trial in June 2027
At least 30 people were killed in a Russian strike on a bus in eastern Ukraine, a day after another Russian strike killed 22 people in an apartment building
The attacks come as Russia intensifies its use of drones, missiles, and guided bombs against Ukrainian targets

It could reach Category 3 strength, prompting hurricane watches and mandatory evacuations in parts of Florida

What they didn’t anticipate was what the U.S. would do to get there , Rafaela Jinich writes

title: Anne Carson’s Seductive Strangeness
excerpt: Anne Carson, who won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature today, doesn’t write masterpieces or door-stoppers, and she has no interest in emulating the great works
body: Anne Carson, who won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature today, doesn’t write masterpieces or door-stoppers, and she has no interest in emulating the great works of the past—including those of past laureates
Despite her training as a classicist and her celebrated skill as a translator, she would likely have little to say about the authenticity of film adaptations of The Odyssey
Carson is a poet by trade, but she’s really an archaeologist of sorts, sifting through the pottery shards of culture and letting the light of our own time illuminate their beauty

Carson prefers to use fragments as seeds for her own poetry, and the high-cultural touchpoints for her lyrics and critical essays—Sappho, Samuel Beckett, Franz Kafka, Michelangelo Antonioni, Simone Weil—sometimes give her work an air of forbidding experimentation that quickly turns, upon reading, into pleasure and delight
You may not know or care who Heloïse and Abelard are, but I can promise that you will enjoy reading them argue in a hotel room in the middle of her 2005 “spoken-word opera,” Decreation

Across roughly two dozen translations and original books, a twee-punk “don’t give a damn” attitude pervades Carson’s reinterpretation of ancient texts: Her poetry shuns obeisance to tradition and literality and embraces creative fantasy instead
For that reason, the barrier to entry for her poetry is surprisingly low—surprisingly, I mean, for a poet whose books often contain a page or two of footnotes
Carson wrote a Ph.D. dissertation on the ancient poet Sappho at the University of Toronto, in the city where she was born in 1950
When I was a classics major in college, her 1998 re-creation of a bit of obscure Greek mythology, Autobiography of Red , was a cult object
Some of her poetry isn’t even poetry at all, but a mix of essays, screenplays, even the odd oratorio
Nox , her 2010 elegy for her brother—the title is Latin for “night”—arrives in a box and unfolds like an accordion

Carson’s predilection for the classics doesn’t domesticate them; it riffs on how astonishingly strange it can be to put words down on a page (or papyrus) in a meaningful order, and to try to have them capture the human condition. [ Read: The best American poetry of the 21st century (so far) ] Sappho , Carson’s early subject, offers an important clue as to why her work matters to us now, and perhaps also as to why she won the Nobel
Sappho’s poetry has survived only in bits and pieces, and her form of writing, as much as her obsession with love and longing, has inspired Carson’s own iconoclastic, restless tacking among genres
Yet Carson is averse to the common assumption that we have to look for what’s directly relatable in the past in order to fall in love with it

In an interview with The Paris Review , she confessed that she finds very little “direct relevance of ancient things to modern things”; instead, she gets “little glimpses of similarity, embedded in unbelievable otherness.” That strikes me as pretty close to a definition of poetry itself, the art form that may be better than any other at embedding everyday objects (a wheelbarrow, a coffee spoon) within the tantalizing atmosphere of the new

Carson’s poetry connects us to the past for the same reason that it stands out as some of the most accomplished poetry of her generation : Rather than lulling us with history’s familiarity, she seduces us with its strangeness
In the days leading up to the Nobel Prize announcement, I happened to have been rereading Autobiography of Red for the first time in 24 years
This “novel in verse” takes its prompt from a 6th-century-B.C.E. fragment about a little monster, Geryon, who falls in love with Herakles—before the god kills him
In Carson’s rendering, the two meet as teenagers at a bus station and reunite years later in Buenos Aires
They travel by plane to a volcano in Peru, where Geryon, now an aspiring photographer, takes pictures of the bubbling lava (no one dies)

From so fragile, bizarre, and slender a source—we never forget this is a meet-cute between a red, winged monster and a divine hero—Carson conjures a romance in which love feels unbelievably alien and yet utterly recognizable: “Up on the overpass / the night was wide open / and blowing headlights like a sea

He stood against the wind and let it peel him / clean.” Carson’s playfulness, humor, and curiosity—and, above all, her tenderness—make her poetry a powerful antidote to the chilled and coarsened social world of the present, not to mention the worry that history and the classics will lose their audiences
What I find most moving about her work is her ability to turn abstract thought into concrete feeling, and to make this feeling our own

Who has not wondered, as the young Geryon does, what “distance” looks like? Carson writes, “It extends from a spaceless within to the edge of what can be loved.” When I gaze down a path or a road, when I feel the separation from someone I love, or when I think of the gulf between the present and the past, I somehow know exactly what she means.

title: The Oil Crisis America Saw Coming
excerpt: This is an edition of Time-Travel Thursdays, a journey through The Atlantic ’s archives to contextualize the present
body: This is an edition of Time-Travel Thursdays, a journey through The Atlantic ’s archives to contextualize the present
In December 1987, The Atlantic had some reassuring news for readers: The next oil crisis didn’t have to happen
The United States had already endured the oil shocks of the 1970s, and Amory B
Hunter Lovins, a pair of then-married environmentalists, argued in this magazine that the country had learned from the experience

The U.S. had diversified its sources of foreign oil, and the American economy needed less oil to grow, a shift that the Lovinses attributed mainly to efficiency gains, such as better-insulated buildings and more fuel-efficient cars
Oil production had grown outside OPEC, an organization of oil-exporting states, reducing the world’s reliance on Persian Gulf oil
Even the Strait of Hormuz, a flash point in the Iran-Iraq War of the ’80s, appeared less threatening to the global supply

By 1987, less oil was passing through the waterway than earlier in the decade, and the Lovinses believed that reserves and alternative routes could help make up for any sudden cutoffs caused by geopolitical tensions

The moment offered what the writers called a “unique opportunity”: a reprieve from Middle Eastern dominance of the global oil supply. “If this interval is frittered away,” they warned, “it could end with the United States, its alternative options expired, needing Middle Eastern oil more than ever.” Nearly four decades later, America is far less vulnerable to foreign-oil disruptions, but it is once again caught in a global oil crisis, and the Strait of Hormuz is back at the center
Before the Iran war, about a quarter of the world’s maritime oil passed through the strait, roughly three times the daily volume that had passed through in 1987

The effective closure of the waterway has resulted in global oil inventories falling by more than 500 million barrels since February , and Americans are feeling the effects, as the costs of diesel , air travel , food , and other goods all rise
But not all of the Lovinses’ worries have come to pass

America has become far less reliant on foreign oil than it was in the ’80s; the shale boom, precipitated by advances in horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing, unlocked large amounts of domestic oil, transforming the U.S. energy market beginning in the 2000s
Last year, American crude production reached a record 13.6 million barrels a day, and Persian Gulf countries supplied just 8 percent of U.S. crude imports
The contrast with the 1970s is stark: In 1977, the broader group of OPEC countries supplied 85 percent of American crude-oil imports

As my colleague Rogé Karma reported in March, America’s growing energy independence appears to have helped convince the Trump administration ahead of the Iran war that the U.S. could withstand a disruption in the Persian Gulf. “We don’t get any oil anymore out of the Strait of Hormuz,” Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said last October, in defense of America’s decision to strike Iran’s nuclear facilities earlier that year
The Lovinses had imagined a different route to energy security
They called it “substitution”: reducing the need for oil overall by continuing to improve energy efficiency in buildings and vehicles, and replacing oil with natural gas or alternative fuels
They argued that efficiency could buy the country time to free itself from dependence on foreign oil
America ultimately achieved much of that goal, but by producing more oil rather than using less
After OPEC’s 1973 oil embargo, President Richard Nixon launched “Project Independence” with the goal of reducing the country’s reliance on foreign oil

Congress adopted new conservation measures , and Jimmy Carter made reducing energy consumption a centerpiece of his presidency, while also beginning to lift federal controls on oil prices to free up more domestic production
In 1979, Carter went so far as to promise that the country would never again “use more foreign oil” than it had in 1977
Days after taking office, President Ronald Reagan eliminated the remaining federal controls on oil prices
The approach appeared to be working: By the early 1980s, U.S. oil consumption had fallen to its lowest level in more than a decade
But the conditions that encouraged conservation soon changed
Weaker oil demand and growing supply contributed to a glut that sent oil prices plunging in 1986
As oil became cheaper, the economic pressure to conserve diminished, and the efficiency gains of the previous decade began to level off
Reagan’s administration sought deep cuts to federal conservation research, part of a broader retreat from government-led energy programs during the 1980s
Conservation had never been the country’s only answer to the oil shocks
Policy makers were simultaneously trying to increase domestic production and diversify the country’s energy supply

Carter argued in 1979 that the country needed to “produce more” as well as “conserve more.” What ultimately endured was not the ambition to wean the country off oil, but the goal of making America less vulnerable to foreign suppliers

In April, my colleague Idrees Kahloon wrote that the country is at a point where it can administer energy “shocks to other countries without feeling much pain itself,” but Americans have not been spared the effects of an international oil shortage
Gasoline prices still rise with global oil prices, regardless of where the crude comes from
Countries that are more dependent on Gulf energy, meanwhile, have borne more of the disruption
Most of the crude oil passing through Hormuz was headed to Asia , not the United States
The Philippines declared a state of emergency in response to energy shortages, Japan faced higher oil costs, and European countries saw disruptions to natural-gas shipments push prices up
This is not quite the future the Lovinses imagined, but neither is it the one they feared
They understood the calm of the 1980s as a reprieve, not a resolution
Four decades later, the United States has emerged from the crises of the ’70s as the world’s largest oil producer, far less dependent on the Middle East but still dependent on fuel itself

title: What I Saw at New York’s Anti-Israel October 7 Rallies
excerpt: Yesterday was a reminder of the difficulty that the pro-Palestine left has with showing grace even for the dead
body: Yesterday was a reminder of the difficulty that the pro-Palestine left has with showing grace even for the dead

On the third anniversary of the day that Hamas gunmen and freelance killers arrived in Israel on motorcycles and paragliders and trucks, and slaughtered children and grandparents and mothers and fathers and dancing young people, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani put out a statement that was empathetic and modulated in tone … for about 50 words. “This day is profoundly painful for so many New Yorkers,” Mamdani began. “It marks three years since the horrific war crimes of October 7
On that day, Hamas killed more than 1,100 Israelis and abducted 251 others
We grieve alongside our many friends and neighbors who still carry that unthinkable loss.” Alas, then came the next 162 words, as the young mayor indulged his anger with Israel

He apparently felt obligated to give New York City—which is home to the biggest Jewish population of any city on the globe—a history lesson that seemed to suggest that Israel brought the October 7 tragedy upon itself. “The suffering did not begin nor end that day,” he wrote. “It instead continued through the Israeli government’s devastating, ongoing genocide in Gaza, in which it has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians—including more than 21,000 children
Even since the so-called ceasefire, more than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed

That suffering has intensified with every Israeli bomb dropped on ambulances waiting outside hospitals, every drone strike targeting a residential building or journalist, and every shipment of food aid turned away at a border crossing.” [ Jonathan Chait: Progressive activists are sometimes on the wrong side of history ] On he went, referencing Israeli war crimes and apartheid and unbearable grief and American complicity in it all
By the time he concluded, he had turned grace into a cudgel

Ammiel Hirsch, a prominent New York rabbi and a longtime peace advocate, called the statement “morally perverse” and likened it to “sticking a knife into the pain of the Jewish community.” Mamdani might have thought his statement to be provocative enough to satisfy even the most anti-Zionist, anti-Israel leftist
But portions of New York’s pro-Palestine community were insistent about observing the anniversary with a Citywide Protest Resisting Genocide since 1948

They were less intent on remembering Palestinians who have suffered grievously than they were focused on implicitly saluting Hamas’s savage attack, as their call to protest offered “glory to the martyrs, victory to the resistance.” And a fringe went further still, denouncing Mamdani for what it perceived as insufficient anti-Israel fervor
I spent some hours yesterday tracking these protests, including classroom walkouts and marches, and in truth, the numbers were deeply underwhelming
The demonstration began with 80 or so New York University students gathering for a noontime rally in Washington Square Park
They chanted, denounced their university leaders, and listened as an NYU professor spun out various conspiracy theories suggesting that Israel was principally responsible for its own casualties

Two hours later, another 75 or 80 students gathered on Broadway, outside the Columbia University campus, and chanted, “Intifada revolution” and “Palestine from river to sea,” an idea that, as a practical matter, would entail the abolition of Israel
A larger rally was planned at City Hall Park in the late afternoon
Protesters there numbered—and my grading could be generous—a touch more than 200

This included a breakaway group of roughly two dozen anti-Zionist ultra-Orthodox Satmars, a crew of black-clad anarchists who did their best to appear forbidding, and an impressively insistent Maoist Communist faction

The lackluster turnout might have owed in part to the fact that the grandees of New York’s organized left, in particular the New York City chapter of Democratic Socialists of America, were savvy enough to avoid militant protest on this solemn day
The New York City DSA went silent on social media, making no mention of October 7 or the rallies
Only the youth wing of DSA showed up. [ Rose Horowitch: Where are all the campus protests? ] There was a faint hint of anti-Mamdanism
A young protester, his face wrapped in a keffiyeh, shouted into a bullhorn and assayed a brief attack on the mayor
His voice was muffled by the cloth, so it was difficult to make out what he said, save for the fact that he repeated it rhythmically
Perhaps seven or eight protesters joined in, and a Maoist held aloft and jiggled an anti-Mamdani sign
The atmosphere grew more hostile as day turned to night and the protest came to a desultory end
According to news reports, a rump group of perhaps 100 followers of various obscure militant-left groups and pro-Palestine groups marched north from city hall to Union Square
They were intent on disrupting a remembrance run by the anti-war group Israelis for Peace and attended by Mamdani
That vigil recognized both the Israeli dead and the many thousands of Palestinians who have died in the war in Gaza
The protesters crowded in, unleashing boos and chants, not least at Mamdani, whom they appeared to cast as Judas for standing alongside left-wing Jews and very liberal Zionists
Peter Sterne, an editor at City & State New York , posted on X some of their nastier chants: “Traitor, traitor, come on out! You sold all your people out!” and “Zohran, you can’t hide
We charge you with genocide!” Mamdani, accompanied by his police detail, left to a chorus of jeers and boos
A revolution eating its own is a historical commonplace
For now, Mamdani has used his considerable political skills to keep the most uncompromising of his pro-Palestine-left supporters in check
But last night perhaps signaled a fraying of patience.

title: How Digger Dug Its Own Box-Office Grave
excerpt: The following contains spoilers for the film Digger
body: The following contains spoilers for the film Digger
Digger ’s marketing campaign began not with a trailer but with a montage —a reel of previous performances by the movie’s star, Tom Cruise
There was Cruise in Top Gun , feeling the need for speed; Cruise in Jerry Maguire , committing to showing the money; Cruise in the Mission: Impossible films , dangling from various planes

The retrospective ended with a snippet of Cruise acting in Digger , but its message was clear: What the movie star of movie stars pulls off in this forthcoming project would be the pinnacle of Cruise-ian cinema, the performance he’s been building toward all this time
As it turns out, the movie is indeed a historic entry in Cruise’s filmography—though likely not for the reasons anyone involved had hoped
Digger has become one of the worst-performing releases of his career, making roughly $8 million domestically during its opening weekend against a reported budget of up to $180 million
Few reviews are glowing; it also has the unfortunate distinction of being the final film released by Warner Bros. before the company’s acquisition by Paramount, a deal that closed this week
The promotional tone has shifted significantly—no longer are teasers celebrating the opportunity to see Cruise as people have never seen him before
They now offer a more desperate plea: “ Decide for yourself ,” one of the latest ads says, a shrug of a command
That Digger ’s marketing relied so heavily on Cruise’s star power isn’t surprising
But the film’s dramatic bombing at the box office proves the (literal) tomfoolery of making Cruise its only selling point
For years, the actor has adopted the persona of Hollywood’s unofficial mayor, stressing whenever possible the importance of seeing movies in theaters with crowds
Digger , however, has no trace of crowd-pleasing in its DNA

Directed by Alejandro González Iñárritu, it’s a satire of a satire that’s both grandiose and grotesque, with a Russian doll–like story structure: At its center is a shouty black comedy about the apocalypse, which is caused by an oil tycoon named Digger Rockwell (Cruise)

That tale is then revealed to be a play called Fossil Fools being staged by a harried crew and cast; its star, Curtis Markson (also Cruise), is growing anxious about the ethical implications of the show’s conceit, as well as a possible emergency that his daughter is facing
A final twist unveils the play as a retelling of a real story—that the events of Fossil Fools actually happened, give or take a few creative flourishes

Outside the theater, the world is a dystopian nightmare. [ Read: Hollywood’s star power is shifting ] The entire ethos of Cruise’s career thus butts heads dramatically with the film’s complexity and cynicism
Digger gets the most out of Cruise the actor, who delivers a captivating performance while juggling two characters throughout the film
But it can’t mine much out of Cruise the untouchable, one-note movie star
In an interview with GQ , the first cover story with the magazine that Cruise has agreed to in 20 years, he turned every question into an opportunity to wax poetic about the beauty of filmmaking

Despite being given opportunities to reflect on his career and why he’s been drawn to death-defying, larger-than-life roles, Cruise rarely conveyed anything beyond the talking point he kept pushing about “cinema” being his life’s passion. “What I like about cinema,” he said in response to an inquiry about his childhood, “is it is all of us coming together in a room and sharing an experience.” Cruise has made staunch optimism about the movies his public narrative; for him, the theatrical business must and will succeed no matter what challenges befall the industry. “Hollywood has always gone through ups and downs,” he told GQ . “If you study Hollywood, they’ve been bust and bank and broke
I’m very excited about where movies are.” But Digger displays no such certainty
Rather, it argues that although art can endure the end of the world, overstating the importance of entertainment is silly
Fossil Fools , after all, is funded by a descendant of Digger Rockwell himself

A credit sequence further emphasizes the story’s pessimism by sounding the same warning that the theatergoers hear when the stage show ends; the real-life audience watching Digger is therefore encouraged to brace for a crisis as it leaves the building as well
Digger isn’t the only film this year underlining the bleak world we’re in

Both The Social Reckoning , the writer-director Aaron Sorkin’s follow-up to The Social Network , and Artificial , the auteur Luca Guadagnino’s movie about the founding of OpenAI, are tonally different from Digger , but they contend with the same challenge Digger does: persuading audiences to spend a few hours in a theater absorbing disturbing stories about a reality they already know

The two movies also seem to face uphill box-office battles, despite featuring acclaimed actors: The former, starring the recent Oscar winner Mikey Madison, is on track for a soft opening this weekend, while the latter, with Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman, was dropped by its original distributor, Amazon MGM Studios; a smaller company, Neon, rescued the project
But even if these films also fail to become hits, at least they’re not hiding their messages behind the charm of their stars.

title: The Download: AI roadblocks for humanoids and portable rubber dams
excerpt: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
AI breakthroughs in robotics won’t change your life any time soon The hype around humanoid robots is reaching fever pitch
Much of it comes from the idea that the same AI advances behind ChatGPT and Claude could enable robots to imitate human movement the way chatbots imitate human language
They argue that such assumptions minimize the challenges of using an intelligence built on language and images to master the infinite variability of the physical world
They also point out that conflating humanoids with so-called generalist machines is misleading
Across robotics labs, tensions have emerged over whether current forms of AI are all that’s needed to perfect all-purpose humanoids or whether an entirely new path is required

Read the full story on what it will take to build truly general-purpose robots . —Jamie Condliffe This story is a collaboration between MIT Technology Review and Aventine , a non-profit research foundation that creates and supports content about how technology and science are changing the way we live. 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: WaveSave and its portable rubber dam WaveSave is one of MIT Technology Review’s 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch 2026 , available exclusively to subscribers
As sea levels rise and flood risks worsen, WaveSave has emerged with an ingeniously simple tool: a portable rubber dam that’s quick to install when flooding starts
Anyone can unfurl the SlamDam on the ground along a riverbank or shoreline and pump it full of water until it swells into place

And there it stands, up to 1.3 meters high, shielding nearby property or structures from damage as waters rise.  WaveSave now plans to take its unusual approach to flood protection much further . —Amy Nordrum Subscribers can now access the full 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch , spanning everything from smart turbines and sustainable cement to carbon dioxide batteries

Why we’re watching these climate tech companies —Casey Crownhart Our Climate Tech Companies to Watch list is always a little ray of hope for me—there are some fascinating ideas out there about how we power our world or move away from fossil fuels.  Our chosen companies also reflect several aspects of the current moment
One is that China is the center of the climate and energy tech world
Another is that everybody wants a piece of the data center pie
And then there’s the fact that the grid needs support, with energy storage a key piece moving forward

Ultimately, it has one big choice to make: adopt a conservative strategy that aims to preserve its lead for the next five years—or orient itself toward genuine computing moonshots
There is no shortage of candidates, including quantum computing, neuromorphic computing and reversible computing
And there are plenty of novel materials and devices
These possibilities could even be combined to form hybrid computing systems
The National Semiconductor Technology Center can drive these ideas forward
To be successful, it would do well to follow DARPA’s lead by focusing on moonshot programs
