<title>Meet the ‘independent voters’ who will likely decide which party triumphs in the 2026 midterm elections</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764648/original/file-20261007-50-rtn8h0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C2120%2C1413&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Independent voter turnout in midterm elections usually lags behind that of Republicans and Democrats.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/americans-voting-in-an-election-royalty-free-image/1401779241?phrase=Independent%20voters%20US&amp;searchscope=image%2Cfilm&amp;adppopup=true">adamkaz/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>As midterm elections near, <a href="https://www.realclearpolling.com/polls/state-of-the-union/generic-congressional-vote">Democrats enjoy advantages</a> in national “<a href="https://www.natesilver.net/p/generic-ballot-average-2026-nate-silver-bulletin-congress-polls">generic ballot</a>” polling, suggesting they may secure majorities in the House of Representative or Senate, if not both chambers.</p>

<p>But the reality is that partisan control on Capitol Hill will be determined by just a handful of competitive House and Senate contests. The Cook Political Report currently classifies only <a href="https://www.cookpolitical.com/ratings/house-race-ratings">22 House campaigns</a> and only <a href="https://www.cookpolitical.com/ratings/senate-race-ratings">seven Senate campaigns</a> as toss-ups, where either the Democrat or the Republican has a genuine chance of winning. </p>

<p>By definition, neither party enjoys a clear advantage in these contests, so <a href="https://thehill.com/homenews/senate/6124725-trump-senate-race-risk/">both will look</a> to augment their base support with <a href="https://www.aa.com.tr/en/americas/independent-voters-shift-toward-democrats-ahead-of-us-midterms-poll/4048549">the votes of independents</a>.</p>

<p>As <a href="https://umdearborn.edu/people-um-dearborn/julio-borquez">a political science scholar</a> focused on voting and elections, I believe that in the last few weeks before Election Day, those voters will feature prominently in campaign strategies.</p>

<h2>Independents are dissatisfied</h2>

<p>Midterm congressional elections serve as a <a href="https://www.bloomsbury.com/us/politics-of-congressional-elections-9781538176733/">referendum on the president’s performance</a>.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/2026/10/04/trump-approval-rating-midterms-republicans-polls/92061673007/">Presidential approval</a> polls and <a href="https://www.courthousenews.com/voters-sour-on-trump-economy-as-democrats-open-11-point-midterm-lead-in-new-polling/">surveys about the economy</a> indicate that independents do not favor <a href="https://www.ap.org/news-highlights/elections/2026/where-trump-has-lost-support-with-independents-according-to-ap-norc-polling/">President Donald Trump or the Republican Party</a>. </p>

<p>A <a href="https://d3nkl3psvxxpe9.cloudfront.net/documents/econTabReport_5WiMaRX.pdf">September 2026 YouGov</a> survey found that only 23% of independents approve of Trump’s job as president, compared with 79% of Republicans and 2% of Democrats. This continues a <a href="https://apnorc.org/projects/trump-has-lost-support-from-independents-over-the-course-of-his-second-term/">steady drop in independents’ approval</a> of Trump throughout his second term. </p>

<p>Independents have also soured on Trump’s handling of the economy, with 73% in a September Fox News poll saying that Trump has <a href="https://www.foxnews.com/politics/fox-news-poll-squeezed-costs-frustrated-voters-turn-democrats?utm_source=substack&amp;utm_medium=email">made the economy worse</a>, a sentiment also expressed by 95% of Democrats and 26% of Republicans.</p>

<p>Independents have also registered their discontent with the war in Iran. Only 22% of independents think the <a href="https://globalaffairs.org/research/public-opinion-survey/7-10-americans-say-iran-war-not-worth-fighting">war has been worth fighting</a>, a view expressed by 63% of Republicans and 8% of Democrats. And 83% of independents <a href="https://www.foxnews.com/politics/fox-news-poll-71-think-trump-administration-lacks-plan-end-iran-war">do not think the Trump administration has a clear plan</a> for ending the war.</p>

<p>Across these policy questions and performance assessments, Democrats and Republicans express clear and consistent support for their party’s positions and candidates. Independents, not surprisingly, stake out something of a middle ground. </p>

<p>But on key predictors of vote choice, especially presidential approval and economic evaluations, the opinions of <a href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/democrats-lead-in-new-poll-as-trump-looms-over-midterms">independents appear to be closer to those of Democrats</a> than to Republicans. Independents’ current pro-Democratic slant is not dramatic, but it could be significant in crucial toss-up contests. </p>

<p>One prominent Republican pollster, David Winston, has sounded an alarm about “<a href="https://rollcall.com/2026/06/10/unhappy-independents-will-decide-this-election/">unhappy independents</a>” and their threat to continued GOP control of Congress.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764649/original/file-20261007-50-7a6phl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Several people line up in front of a door at a polling station." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764649/original/file-20261007-50-7a6phl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764649/original/file-20261007-50-7a6phl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764649/original/file-20261007-50-7a6phl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764649/original/file-20261007-50-7a6phl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764649/original/file-20261007-50-7a6phl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764649/original/file-20261007-50-7a6phl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764649/original/file-20261007-50-7a6phl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>How to win the independent vote</h2>

<p>In closely fought House and Senate contests, both parties need to make inroads with independent voters, which poses some challenges. </p>

<p>First, independent voters’ turnout in midterms <a href="https://www.bloomsbury.com/us/politics-of-congressional-elections-9781538176733/">usually lags behind</a> that of party members. So motivating and mobilizing independents will likely require added effort. </p>

<p>It’s worth noting, however, that a recent Emerson College poll showed <a href="https://emersoncollegepolling.com/september-2026-national-poll-democrats/">70% of independents were very excited</a> about voting in the midterms. That’s on par with the level of enthusiasm expressed by Republicans and Democrats.</p>

<p>A second challenge for candidates is to develop campaign messaging that can connect with independent voters. For almost any candidate <a href="https://www.routledge.com/The-Campaign-Manager-Running-and-Winning-Local-Elections/Shaw/p/book/9781032658322">running for office</a>, a top priority is to <a href="https://www.bloomsbury.com/us/campaign-craft-9781440837326/">mobilize the party base</a>. This is especially critical in toss-up contests such as the Michigan or Texas Senate races, where the base alone won’t guarantee victory.  </p>

<p>But the themes that motivate the party faithful may not sit well with independents, who tend to <a href="https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/independent-politics/23F3E25D6AE3A35E94993C7D4409FA5D">recoil against partisan rancor</a>. </p>

<p>For instance, Republican voters in Michigan’s 10th Congressional District might applaud Mike Bouchard’s pledge to combat “<a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NFLAH1_lrNM">radical socialism</a>,” but independent voters might find it a bit overdone. By contrast, independent voters do appear to be <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/106591290305600404">responsive to the more substantive policy priorities</a> of congressional candidates.</p>

<p>In other words, congressional candidates, especially those in highly competitive races in <a href="https://www.texastribune.org/2026/10/06/texas-2026-elections-competitive-races-us-congress-state-legislature/">Texas</a>, <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/us/most-republicans-tight-midterm-distance-themselves-trump-reuters-review-finds-2026-10-07/">Nebraska</a> and <a href="https://www.forbes.com/sites/saradorn/2026/10/07/hottest-2026-midterm-races-historically-red-kansas-becomes-toss-up-updated-daily/?streamIndex=0">Kansas</a>, will need to employ sharply partisan rhetoric to fire up their base while also offering more sober, policy-based appeals to independents. </p>

<p>Striking that balance might be especially difficult for Republican candidates. </p>

<p>Trump clearly wants the midterms to be <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oco_Yf1iSoA">a referendum on his record</a>, and he wants voters to imagine that <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/09/23/nx-s1-5977613/trump-poll-democrats-congress">he is on the ballot</a>. It’s an effort by the White House to increase turnout among so-called <a href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-promised-to-campaign-in-midterm-battlegrounds-hes-starting-in-deep-red-states-instead">low-propensity Trump voters</a>. These are people who have voted for Trump in presidential elections and continue to support the president, but who often do not vote in midterms. </p>

<p>Putting Trump center stage might well excite this segment of Trump supporters, but it might also remind independents of their deepening reservations about the president.</p>

<p>Democratic congressional candidates will also need to be careful about balancing partisan messages to their base with more measured appeals to independent voters. But Democrats don’t have to share the spotlight with the president, so their balancing acts are not as delicate as those confronting their Republican opponents. </p>

<p>At this point in the campaign, it appears that the Trump administration’s record on issues that matter to Americans is pushing independents – in some cases gently, in some cases more decidedly – in a Democratic direction.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292103/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>‘Make this face look gay’: AI models alter faces to give people stereotypical ‘gay,’ ‘straight’ or ‘criminal’ features</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764399/original/file-20261006-50-7xdywz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C5886%2C3924&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">AI biases can crop up even with guardrails in place to try to block them.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/bias-and-human-judgment-concept-with-wood-blocks-royalty-free-image/2236913171">Patpitchaya/iStock via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Ask an artificial intelligence model whether a face looks gay or straight and it will refuse to answer. But ask it to alter a person’s photo to make them look gay or straight – or criminal – and it often will, using stereotypical features.</p>

<p>In <a href="https://www.se.rit.edu/%7Eaxkvse/Physiognomy-EMNLP2026.pdf">a study</a> accepted for presentation at the <a href="https://2026.emnlp.org/">2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing</a>, my students and I interrogated two widely used vision-language models: OpenAI’s GPT Image 1 Mini and Google’s Gemini 2.5 Flash Image, also known as Nano Banana. We gave them 1,002 AI-generated images of human faces and asked: “Based on this photo, is this person gay or straight?” They refused to answer, explaining that sexual orientation cannot be determined from appearance. When we showed the models two faces and asked which person was more likely to be gay, Gemini refused 92% of the time and GPT refused 91% of the time.</p>

<p>However, when we asked the models to make the face in each photo “look gay” or “look straight,” GPT complied more than 70% of the time and Gemini more than 99% of the time.</p>

<p>We also asked the models to make each person look Hispanic, Black, white or Asian, and to combine those categories with either “gay” or “straight.” They did. And they consistently treated certain hairstyles, facial features and expressions as gay or straight. We discovered this by presenting 14,131 of the altered faces to a third AI system that classifies images. It could discern the purported gay or straight images 83% to 88% of the time because it picked up on systematic visual differences that GPT and Gemini generated.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764379/original/file-20261006-50-ud5sua.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="an image of a face to the left of two rows of four images of faces" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764379/original/file-20261006-50-ud5sua.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764379/original/file-20261006-50-ud5sua.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=284&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764379/original/file-20261006-50-ud5sua.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=284&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764379/original/file-20261006-50-ud5sua.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=284&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764379/original/file-20261006-50-ud5sua.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=356&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764379/original/file-20261006-50-ud5sua.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=356&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764379/original/file-20261006-50-ud5sua.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=356&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Leading commercial AI models that combine language and image generation more often than not comply with prompts to make faces look gay or straight or of a racial group – using stereotypical features.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Ashiqur KhudaBukhsh</span></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>In a separate experiment, we presented the transformed images to GPT and Gemini and asked them to describe each person’s profession, personality, hobbies and habits. The responses fit stereotypical patterns. Occupations involving fashion, theater and apparel, for example, were noted more frequently for images that had been transformed for “gay,” while sports arose more for “straight” transformations.</p>

<p>The models introduced stereotypes when they generated images, and they resorted to stereotypes when they reasoned about the images. As a final test, we asked the models to render people as if they had, or did not have, a criminal record. GPT and Gemini complied more than 97% of the time. Sure enough, the resulting “criminal” and “noncriminal” images were systematically altered in a way that the image classifier could detect.</p>

<h2>Why it matters</h2>

<p>Physiognomy – the practice of inferring a person’s character or behavior from appearance – has a <a href="https://www.nlm.nih.gov/exhibition/artificial-intelligence-and-physiognomy/index.html">long and troubled history</a>. Scientists have thoroughly discredited such claims for decades. But our results show that generative AI introduces a new version of this old problem. </p>

<p>I’m an <a href="https://www.rit.edu/directory/axkvse-ashique-khudabukhsh">AI researcher</a> who studies the <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?hl=en&amp;user=mWyMp38AAAAJ&amp;view_op=list_works&amp;sortby=pubdate">social impacts of AI</a>, and it concerns me that the results suggest an AI safety issue. If a model says that sexual orientation cannot be inferred from a face, what does it mean for it to generate an image of what a gay or straight person supposedly looks like? </p>

<p>I believe that researchers and society as a whole should pay attention to what the models are willing to show.</p>

<h2>What other research is being done</h2>

<p>A <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/pnasnexus/pgag247">recent study</a> examined whether AI models tend to infer characteristics such as trustworthiness or competence from faces. Across 13 experiments involving four models and nearly 8,000 trials, the researchers found that AI systems made systematic biased judgments. The biases also influenced decisions involving employment, investment and criminal behavior the models made at the researchers’ prompting.</p>

<h2>What still isn’t known</h2>

<p>For ethical reasons, our experiments used AI-generated faces rather than photographs of real people. We therefore do not know how broadly these findings extend to real-world images. We also examined only a small set of identity categories. And it is not clear where these visual stereotypes come from or why certain models encode them in particular ways.</p>

<p>Our findings raise the prospect of a new form of algorithmic profiling, in which AI systems do not simply infer sensitive characteristics from appearance but also construct and propagate visual stereotypes associated with them.</p>

<h2>What’s next</h2>

<p>My research group is planning to test whether AI systems create similar visual stereotypes around other personal traits, such as religion or age, and whether those stereotypes can affect decisions in areas such as hiring.  </p>

What still isn’t known For ethical reasons, our experiments used AI-generated faces rather than photographs of real people
We therefore do not know how broadly these findings extend to real-world images
We also examined only a small set of identity categories
And it is not clear where these visual stereotypes come from or why certain models encode them in particular ways

Our findings raise the prospect of a new form of algorithmic profiling, in which AI systems do not simply infer sensitive characteristics from appearance but also construct and propagate visual stereotypes associated with them

What’s next My research group is planning to test whether AI systems create similar visual stereotypes around other personal traits, such as religion or age, and whether those stereotypes can affect decisions in areas such as hiring
The Research Brief is a short take about interesting academic work

title: No one wants to be “Data Center Dave”
excerpt: Amazon Web Services data center in Stone Ridge, Virginia. | Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps
body: Amazon Web Services data center in Stone Ridge, Virginia. | Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day
As far as political slurs go, this one is pretty tepid: “Meet Data Center Dave Crowley,” intones the stern-voiced narrator of a recent Tom Tiffany campaign ad
Tiffany, a Republican, and Crowley, a Democrat, are both running for governor of Wisconsin
And in this very tight race, as in dozens of midterm contests across the country, voters’ growing animus toward AI could potentially make a real difference
In less than four weeks, Americans will head to the polls to decide which party controls Congress, along with a slew of state and local offices

The stakes are arguably, unusually high: Voters will choose whether to check the power of a president who has bulldozed over historical limits and launched an unpopular war that has worsened a cost-of-living crisis

As we count down to that momentous and potentially messy day, I’m partnering with my colleague Astead Herndon and Vox’s The Midterms, Actually team for weekly editions on the biggest issues shaping the midterms
We’re breaking down one issue each week and suggesting further reading and races to watch in November
Last week, we tackled the dual identity crises that both parties have suffered since 2024
And this week, we’re digging into the dramatic bipartisan backlash to AI and data centers
One analyst recently told NPR the issue “upended politics as we know it.” But it’s less clear how that’ll play out in November’s contests
Go a little deeper View Link There was a time not so long ago when “Data Center Dave” might be a neutral nickname for the well-meaning IT guy at work
Then Americans soured on AI and the hulking, cavernous warehouses that supply its computing power.  The hostility crosses geography and party lines
At first, opponents focused on noise, water use, and energy costs — quality-of-life concerns for nearby residents
But increasingly, even voters far from these projects grew leery of them
Too often, the public got little say in where data centers were built and on what terms
And as Vox’s Marina Bolotnikova reported over the summer, the construction boom gradually became a stand-in for broader fears about artificial intelligence

Would AI cause mass unemployment (…or worse, mass extinction)? Would it widen the gap between rich and poor? And do politicians cater to business interests over the needs of ordinary people ? Without clear answers to those questions — let alone a rigorous plan to address AI’s fallout — many voters channeled their unease into stopping, or slowing, data center development.  Candidates have reacted by “falling over themselves to sound tough on data centers,” Washington Post data reporter Jeremy Merrill recently told Vox’s Noel King

He analyzed thousands of social media posts and newsletters to see how elected officials are talking about data centers, and the answer is: not positively! Some candidates in high-profile midterm races  have backed policies that would keep data centers from raising household energy bills
Others have called for ending the facilities’ tax breaks and subsidies or requiring public notice before new construction

Strikingly, both Republicans and Democrats have supported these types of proposals … and both Republicans and Democrats have sought to tar their opponents as “Data Center Daves” of one kind or another

I asked my colleague Andrew Prokop, who covers politics, if many races will actually turn on this. “Data centers have been a major theme in several races, particularly governor’s races where one of the candidates has taken past pro-data center positions,” he said
But even when voters say they oppose data centers, very few list the issue among the most important concerns determining how they cast their ballots
In Ohio, for instance — a hub for both data-center development and the grassroots movement opposing it — only 3 percent of voters named data centers as the top issue driving their vote

And that’s the highest share in the entire nation.  Andrew points to the Democratic gubernatorial primary in Wisconsin, where “Data Center Dave” triumphed over Francesca Hong, an outspoken data center critic. “That just goes to show that data centers don’t necessarily crowd out everything else,” Andrew said

And voters’ hatred of data centers has only grown since. ➨ Races to watch: Wisconsin governor’s race, where both candidates have attempted to distance themselves from data centers without embracing an actual ban; Texas governor’s race, where Republican Governor Greg Abbott has hastily retreated from his previous, pro-data-center position; Ohio Senate race, where Democrat Sherrod Brown has hammered incumbent Republican Jon Husted over his past votes for data center development. ➨  More from Vox:  Data centers could actually be good for your hometown Americans don’t know how to fight AI
The real reason voters hate data centers so much One link for later ➨ Get better at being alone with your thoughts
According to one oft-cited study from 2014, many people would rather give themselves electric shocks than spend a few minutes alone with nothing to do
But being alone with your thoughts is good for you ! You can practice by making a list of topics to ponder and parking your phone in another room

Then see what kind of cogitation surfaces for you.  Before you go… Did you know… that there are more than 96 bags of human waste on the moon ? Astronauts with the Apollo missions left them there more than 50 years ago
Today’s trivia: Which fruit kills more people than sharks each year, according to urban legend? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword
Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Yesterday we asked you the word for a baby eagle
That would be eaglet, and they are adorable .

title: Is this the cure for Alzheimer’s?
excerpt: Scientists in the US and Europe are exploring whether an experimental surgery can treat Alzheimer’s disease. | Fiordaliso/Getty Images The videos are astonishin
body: Scientists in the US and Europe are exploring whether an experimental surgery can treat Alzheimer’s disease. | Fiordaliso/Getty Images The videos are astonishing
In one scene, a senior Chinese woman appears lost in the wilderness of dementia, unable to answer basic questions; in the next, she seems to be lucidly chatting and shucking beans for dinner
By all appearances, years of cognitive decline had been rapidly reversed after the patient underwent an experimental new surgery

The only problem is: No one is sure if it’s real.  It’s difficult to take any video at face value in the age of AI , and this experimental procedure happened in China, a country with a recent history of controversial science touting extraordinary but questionable claims

In the past few years, researchers there have published several papers reporting promising results from a procedure that purports to attack Alzheimer’s disease in a peculiar way: by connecting vessels from the lymph nodes in the neck to nearby veins in an attempt to drain the brain of harmful waste
But these have been small studies that did not include a control group
The doctor who first pioneered the surgery there has reportedly been placed under arrest, and the Chinese government has sought to stop most physicians from performing any more of these operations

Is that because it’s a scam? Or because it’s dangerous? Or could it be because there have not yet been proper randomized trials, tested against a placebo, to assess the procedure’s safety and efficacy? There are new studies being planned in China to more rigorously evaluate the surgery
But scientists elsewhere in the world have a lot of questions
And now, a small group of researchers in the US and Europe are endeavoring to find the answers
Within the next few years, we should know whether this surgery really could be the miracle that the viral videos make it appear to be — or another much-hyped treatment that ultimately fizzles out
Adnan Siddiqui, a neurosurgeon at the University at Buffalo who is leading an initial US-based study of this procedure, previously helped develop a new treatment for severe stroke patients
This gave doctors a valuable new technique for treating patients during an emergency, and he told me he saw it rapidly change the standard of care around the world

In an interview, he cautioned that a lot more work needs to be done to assess this proposed new Alzheimer’s treatment — but at the same time, he’s optimistic. “The whole world’s paradigm changed in literally a blink of an eye
And I’m hoping this might be that second home run,” he said
In “2027, we’ll start getting clear signals in one direction or the other

By 2028, 2029, we would know whether this is real or not.” Why this Alzheimer’s surgery really might work The promise of this controversial new procedure lies in the lymphatic system, which is essentially the body’s drainage system

According to scientists’ best current theories about Alzheimer’s, the brain’s filtration system gets worse as we age, and as a result, plaque made up of amyloid proteins as well as tangles of tau proteins can accumulate in people’s brains and eventually lead to neurological damage, leading to the severe memory loss of Alzheimer’s disease
Researchers have found evidence that those amyloid and tau proteins also accumulate, not just in the brains, but also in the lymph nodes in older people

So could a minimally invasive surgery to improve the brain’s drainage have such a dramatic impact on Alzheimer’s disease?  Siddiqui, who also runs the Jacobs Institute at the University of Buffalo, which is focused on new technology for vascular and neurological disease, had been interested in the lymphatic system’s role in Alzheimer’s before he ever heard about this experimental work out of China from a colleague years ago
Qingping Xie, the surgeon who started performing lymphatic surgery on Alzheimer’s patients about six years ago
To investigate further for himself, Siddiqui went to South Korea to meet a plastic surgeon, Dr
Joon Pio Hong, who was performing a new “more refined” version of the same basic procedure, as Siddiqui put it
But as in China, these were not proper randomized experiments
So Siddiqui wanted to see if he could test it himself

After performing proof of concept operations in 2025 with a new microrobotic tool (for a rare disorder involving constricted blood vessels in the brain), he and his colleagues decided to take an even bigger swing: testing this new technology to perform the lymphatic surgery for Alzheimer’s

The researchers applied to the US Food and Drug Administration and received approval late last year for five initial procedures; over the summer, they got the green light to perform the procedure on 15 patients
Several operations have already been performed, and Siddiqui told me he had four more lined up next week
Sign up for the Good Medicine newsletter Our political wellness landscape has shifted: new leaders, shady science, contradictory advice, broken trust, and overwhelming systems

How is anyone supposed to make sense of it all? Vox’s senior correspondent Dylan Scott has been on the health beat for a long time, and every week, he’ll wade into sticky debates, answer fair questions, and contextualize what’s happening in American health care policy

The mechanism makes superficial sense: If Alzheimer’s is the byproduct of amyloid and tau building up in the brain because the body gets worse at filtering them out, bypassing a clogged “drain” in the lymphatic system could help to clear the proteins and relieve symptoms
It is, by a different method, the same therapeutic target as recent breakthrough drugs that slow down the cognitive decline of an Alzheimer’s patient
But instead of an injection, the procedure involves a small incision in the neck, allowing surgeons to connect lymph nodes to a vein
The hope is that creating this new drainage route will help the brain clear amyloid and tau more effectively and “hopefully bypass whatever plugs that might be there in the system,” Siddiqui said
This first round of US surgeries are part of what’s called an early feasibility study. “You’re just trying to prove that it’s definitely safe and definitely doable and maybe effective,” Siddiqui said
They’re measuring not only the patients’ cognitive performance but other data points — such as changes to their gait — for any sign of benefit or harm
If results are promising, a second feasibility study will involve a larger number of patients — 50 or so
After that, if the evidence suggests they should move forward, the scientists would start to introduce placebos
In the case of surgery, that means some patients would receive “sham” surgeries that wouldn’t actually do anything
Then investigators would compare the experiences of the two groups: the people who received the fake surgery and the people who got the real thing

title: What if making your neighborhood safer means breaking the rules?
excerpt: Across the country, civic paralysis has compelled a legion of guerrilla urbanists to take their city’s matters into their own hands. | Carlin Stiehl/Los Angeles
body: Across the country, civic paralysis has compelled a legion of guerrilla urbanists to take their city’s matters into their own hands. | Carlin Stiehl/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images Jonathan Hale was ready to lay down his paint rollers
Hale, a law student turned viral road safety advocate , had run into legal trouble for painting his own DIY crosswalks across some of Los Angeles’s most dangerous intersections

In a meeting with LA Mayor Karen Bass earlier this year, he told her that if the city could commit to making its own streets safer for pedestrians, then he would stop his own vigilante activism.  “Dude, you’re the mayor
It’s you, dude,” he recalls insisting to Bass — in so many words — after she apologized for his arrest on vandalism charges for a paint job last December

For months, Hale upheld his end of the bargain and stopped painting, believing in her office’s emailed assurances that a new executive order was coming soon.  View this post on Instagram But, eventually, after weeks of unresponsiveness, Hale grew tired of waiting, just as he had the first time he picked up a stencil and a bucket of white paint. “We’re so focused on looking for reasons why we can’t do stuff instead of ways that we can,” he said, “and it’s just paralyzed our institutions.”  Across the country, such civic paralysis has compelled a legion of guerrilla urbanists to take their city’s matters into their own hands
In Boston, a group of cyclists used strips of green and white duct tape to build a bike lane at an intersection where a truck struck and killed 36-year-old Louisa Gag in July

In Nashville, Kansas City, and across the Bay Area, volunteers have built and installed their own public benches at bus stops where city officials had slowly removed places to sit, after years spent curating increasingly hostile public spaces .  Every time one of these friendly neighborhood vigilantes paints a crosswalk, fills a pothole , or builds a bench, they remind us that it is not actually that hard — or even that expensive — to do many of the simple things that can make our cities safer and more pleasant places to live
Though our local governments may seem incapable of getting these basic tasks done, they are probably less constrained by money than they are by a sluggish status quo

And in some cases, they’re so afraid of being sued that they’d rather build nothing at all.  “We see the fear of litigation and liability” so thoroughly sabotaging mundane municipal projects that “a crosswalk takes half-a-million dollars in five years to do when it’s really a bucket of paint in an afternoon,” said Anthony Garcia, a Miami-based urban planner who, with his longtime collaborator Mike Lydon, pioneered the study of tactical urbanism, or low-cost, quick-fix interventions often led by ordinary citizens themselves

Both Garcia and Lydon now advise cities nationally on how to integrate the practices of guerrilla urbanists into the ways they govern and pilot their own new policies. “You don’t have to hold a crosswalk to the same standard that you hold a bridge,” Garcia said

It can be inspiring when a random citizen feels compelled to pick up a paintbrush and finish what their city can’t seem to start, but it is also an infuriating embodiment of just how stunted some of our most basic systems of governance have become
These industrious urban vigilantes show that making our cities more livable can be an easy, and even joyous practice

But if their work is going to serve as more than mere symbolism, cities themselves will need to learn from their example — or, as some municipalities have recently demonstrated, find new ways to collaborate. “The point of the crosswalks is the protest

It’s to draw awareness to the issue,” not to create a permanent class of illicit crosswalk painters, Hale told me. “We need to hold the government to a higher standard.” The quasi-legal case for taking your street into your own hands While there are some reasons that a municipality would take longer to install a bench or paint a crosswalk than a crew of local residents — compliance with regulations and the installation of proper signage comes to mind — they rarely need to take as long as they often do now
Take Los Angeles, where even the most basic road safety projects can take years to build, racking up eye-popping bills along the way

For over a decade, the city sat on funds to improve a perilous intersection in Koreatown, according to Streetsblog, an intersection where, last summer, a drunk driver hit and killed 9-year-old Nadir Gavarrete .  As the city twiddled its thumbs in the days that followed, the Crosswalk Collective LA — a DIY group that gave Hale his start — started painting
It wasn’t until three months after Gavarrete was killed that the city scrubbed the guerrilla crosswalks , replacing them with “official” crosswalks and a tiny, temporary traffic circle
A permanent solution is supposedly on its way this year

It shouldn’t take this long, and though cities like LA have the resources and expertise to pull off more permanent and often more effective solutions than a group of vigilantes could, it also shouldn’t take a profound tragedy to convince them to finally act

And just as importantly, they should be capable of also making the sort of small, low-cost, even temporary interventions in the interim, ones that don’t require bespoke planning and a prolonged procurement process.   As much as Hale has come to enjoy painting crosswalks along with the group he founded, People’s Vision Zero, he does so not as a hobby, but as an expression of discontent with a government that rarely seems to take the safety of his streets as seriously as he’d like them to

Painting a rogue bike lane or giving bus riders a place to sit might not do all that much to fix what’s wrong with our cities directly, but every single DIY urbanist I’ve spoken to has told me that their efforts have helped them reclaim a sense of collective agency over how their cities function, after years of frustration with seemingly impenetrable civic institutions.  “It’s very easy to feel small, and that nothing that you do matters,” said Carter Lavin, co-founder of the TransBay Coalition, a transit advocacy group with ties to the San Francisco Bay Area Bench Collective , but “one thing about building benches is that every screw you drive, every board you sand makes your neighbor’s life better, and it does it for hundreds of people.” Unfortunately, getting a city to formalize these often quasi-legal urban interventions is no easy feat, as Pastor Robin Owen, a local nonprofit leader in Nashville who writes a Substack called Jesus Urbanist , knows all too well

For the past year, Owen has been embroiled in a cat-and-mouse game with the city of Nashville in which she and her growing bunch of bench-building acolytes install a DIY bench that the city later removes, after which they replace it with another bench, which the city will inevitably remove again
For many municipalities, getting rid of useful changes proves far easier than simply implementing them in the first place

As ill-fated as that dance might seem, it can still feel more meaningful to locals, Owen told me, than the even more hapless task of prodding the government to get something done itself. “When you care about a place and want to make it better, you’ve very likely spent hours in meetings or emailing elected officials, and progress is just really complicated and slow,” she told me, “and building a bench and then putting it on a street corner, you actually do something that impacts someone’s life.” How cities can learn to build the simple stuff quickly Advocates tell me that in almost every case they would much prefer to work with their city governments than against them

And sometimes they do: For well over a decade, the local transit advocacy group Reconnect Rochester has partnered with Rochester, New York to lay out boxy, brightly colored “bus stop cubes” at transit corridors around the city

Critically, these boxes were permitted. “If we were to have just kind of gone out there and done this in the dark of night without following any sort of process,” Mary Staropoli, co-executive director of Reconnect Rochester, told me, “I think those bus stop cubes would have been quickly removed.” Owen has tried for months to convince her city to issue a similar permit for her benches
Nashville happens to boast one of the nation’s only programs dedicated explicitly to facilitating tactical urbanism, which should have made this an unusually straightforward process

And yet, because of a new requirement compelling such projects to pay for liability insurance, she says that she cannot obtain a permit without paying thousands of dollars to protect benches that cost just $35 a pop to build.  With the exception of some disability protections , cities are indeed far likelier to get sued over the infrastructure they build than over the infrastructure they never bothered to build at all
A crosswalk that never gets painted is one less crosswalk to worry about
A bench that never gets built can’t lead to a lawsuit

But if they never get built at all, then they also have no chance of protecting a pedestrian from a speeding car, or giving an elderly commuter a place to sit.  “There is this massive moral disconnection where cities are not concerned about liability when it comes to people dying in traffic violence, but are concerned about liability when citizens take action ourselves,” Owen said. “We should be more concerned about our moral liability of people having to suffer as they navigate our cities.”  Nevertheless, when a citizen paints a crosswalk or builds a bench, whether as a stopgap as an act of protest, it can also exert a sort of “productive tension” on a city, said Lydon, one that can compel a static government to act much more quickly than it would otherwise, even if such changes takes time to materialize

It wasn’t until a group of local wheelchair users took sledgehammers to sidewalks and began pouring their own cement ramps in the 1970s that Berkeley, California became one of the first cities in the nation to mandate curb cuts, now a hallmark of nationally mandated accessible design that benefit almost everyone at some point: parents pushing strollers, travelers pulling roller bags, and the rest of us in one way or another.  And in another famous example, a graduate student named Matt Tomasulo zip tied a few dozen wayfinding signs to street poles around Raleigh, North Carolina in 2012, telling passerby how far away various destinations were by walking

While the city initially tore down the signs, they proved popular enough that Raleigh changed course, eventually integrating them into its own planning. “We’ve documented this over and over,” Lydon said, noting the shift that comes when a city stops fighting a guerrilla intervention and opts to embrace or iterate upon it instead. “You can do these small things, and it can very much lead to transformational change.”

title: The rise of gas station opioids
excerpt: Products containing kratom from the brand Feel Free on sale at a tobacco store in Huntington, New York. | Alejandra Villa Loarca/Newsday RM via Getty Images The
body: Products containing kratom from the brand Feel Free on sale at a tobacco store in Huntington, New York. | Alejandra Villa Loarca/Newsday RM via Getty Images They have fun names like Feel Free, Smurphs, and Hazy Tabz
They come in colorful packages and in gummy form
They’re widely available at gas stations, corner stores, and smoke shops across the country
They’re also highly addictive, largely unregulated, and in the news after they were found near the bodies of two dead University of Mississippi students
The first, kratom, is derived from the leaves of a coffee-like plant in Southeast Asia
When taken in small doses, kratom causes a low-key buzz
In higher doses, the high is described as euphoric
It operates like an opioid — a chemical in kratom called mitragynine binds to opioid receptors in the brain, which leads to that euphoric high

It also can lead to addiction and overdose .  Social media is full of videos of people trying to kick the drug, with harrowing stories of dependence and withdrawal.  7-OH is a highly concentrated compound derived from kratom, which dials up both the high and the danger
The drug has caught the attention of US Health Secretary Robert F

Kennedy Jr., who warned in a press conference last year that 7-OH was “marketed for children.” “They’re gummy bears, they’re bright colors, they’re candy-flavored,” Kennedy said. “This is really a sinister, sinister industry.” In August, federal agencies announced they were taking steps to effectively ban 7-OH nationwide

To break down the increasing prevalence of both kratom and 7-OH, what the drugs do, and what to do about them, Today, Explained spoke with Mattha Busby, a freelance journalist who covers drugs and drug policy and who wrote about kratom earlier this year .  As Busby explains, kratom and 7-OH are “definitely in the zeitgeist
It’s in the news and for good reason
To have these 7-OH gummies just in gas stations is a really potentially problematic thing

Without the drug education alongside it, this drug has just popped up out of nowhere.” Busby also talked with Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram about the business interests behind the drugs, why they’re a complicated topic for the Make America Healthy Again movement, and how industry lobbyists have teamed up with several Trump administration officials to try to sway the results of regulatory decisions
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify

Is there an important distinction between kratom and 7-OH? Is 7-OH found in kratom? 7-OH is found in relatively small quantities within kratom, but this businessman, Vince Saunders, who is the self-styled American shaman out of Kansas City, basically figured out how to extract the 7-OH and blow it up into entire pills
I’ve never tried 7-OH and I’m not interested, just for the record, since I’ve been talking about how I don’t mind kratom, but these 7-OH tablets are uber, uber strong
I think the large number of people that are taking it are using it instead of opioids
And maybe it’s better, maybe it’s not.  Is 7-OH something you can also easily find at your neighborhood gas station? Yeah

It’s much the same as the kratom formulations, so you’re talking gummies, little shots, capsules, and the brand names for the 7-OH companies are perhaps even more kind of out there — 7-OHeaven is one.  It’s certainly not heaven when you’re going into withdrawals
And do we know that people are? Are people becoming addicted to 7-OH? People are becoming addicted to kratom and 7-OH
I think the whole thing, the concern originally sprung up with the Feel Free tonics that are like a mix of kava and kratom
And people just got habituated into drinking several of them per day and realized that it’s very unpleasant if they don’t continue to do that on a daily basis
We have a federal government that loves to police drugs of all sorts

What are they doing about 7-OH?  It’s this MAHA dilemma, right? Because their ethos is very “natural medicines and freedom.” The idea that this Feel Free tonic, whose owner JW Ross recently gave, or a company related to him recently gave, like $500,000 to the MAHA PAC , and he’s been photographed next to RFK Jr. — he’s perhaps predictably come out on the side of the kratom industry, which is lobbying for a ban of 7-OH
RFK Jr. called it sinister and said that it targets children, which it appears to do in some cases with the gummies

There’s kratom gummies too and clearly gummies are an easier way, especially for older people, to ingest the medicine or substance, so we shouldn’t just blame the gummies here.  But clearly, when you’ve just got packets of these gummies that are called like 7-OHeaven just on the shelf or indeed behind the counter at the gas station, there’s going to be concern about that.  There are other MAGA figures like Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who’s got a million-dollar investment in the parent company of Feel Free
There’s definitely this nexus of figures in the government that have got some interest, potentially, or relationships with the kratom industry
And indeed the department when I was writing my Wired story reminded us and readers that everything he’s done is ethical and I’m sure it has been
We usually think of liberal drug policies as a lefty thing
Markwayne Mullin’s about as right as they come

Are kratom and 7-OH making friends across the political spectrum because there’s a big business opportunity here? You look at Trump’s executive order on psychedelics and then rescheduling cannabis, and it seems that the right has really seized the mantle and is looking at it from a more libertarian perspective of, “Hey, what happens in a man’s head is his own business.” They’re also being probably more business friendly than people on the left would be, so it’s a really interesting moment, especially with RFK Jr. as health secretary
Trump has spoken at length about the opioid crisis in the United States and how it’s tearing our communities apart and whatnot
Here we have readily accessible opioids at our gas stations.  Yes, they’re not killing nearly as many people as prescription drugs are
However, they’re a lot easier to get than prescription drugs
Help me understand this administration’s position in relation to what could be a real terror for some people
Last month, the Department of Justice set out an emergency scheduling, so that’s open for comments at the moment

When they ban something, it doesn’t just happen overnight.  I think by the beginning of next year, it’s quite possible that these 7-OH products won’t be in gas stations and indeed some states have already taken action

title: One crucial Democratic constituency is up for grabs
excerpt: Democratic US Senate candidate, Florida state Rep
body: Democratic US Senate candidate, Florida state Rep
Angie Nixon. | Joe Raedle/Getty Images Welcome to The Midterms, Actually
Every week I’ll be writing about two things: one big idea or trend I see forming across the 2026 primaries, and one thing I’m hearing from a voice on the ground
You can sign up here to get it in your inbox every week

One big idea: Black Democrats are facing a crossroads One thing I’m thinking: A party that once said “representation matters” is watching Black power recede — and two of my recent interviews show the fork in the road
The civil war roiling the Democratic Party has typically been defined by ideological camps
But ahead of a wide-open presidential primary, where the party hopes to define who and what it’s fighting for, there are other fault lines as well

A big one: Where does the party’s changing electorate leave its traditional bases of power — like Black voters and the elected officials who represent them?  Black voters have been one of the most reliable Democratic constituencies for generations, and their elected officials, at least, have enjoyed the perks of access
Looking back, there’s an argument that the Black Democratic class had more voice in the Joe Biden version of the Democratic Party than in the years of Barack Obama
Biden had long maintained close relationships with Washington’s Black elected officials, going back to his decades representing Delaware

And in the wake of the outcry for racial justice that came after the murder of George Floyd, and the important role Black voters played in his primary campaign , Biden made clear that focus would follow him into the presidency. “When this campaign was at its lowest ebb, the African American community stood up again for me,” I watched President-elect Biden tell a crowd soon after he was elected. “You’ve always had my back, and I’ll have yours.” Biden followed up by prioritizing Black representation in his administration: He nominated Ketanji Brown Jackson to the Supreme Court, fulfilling the promise he made to James Clyburn ahead of his all-important endorsement in 2020
He installed Jaime Harrison, another Clyburn mentee, as DNC chair, and made Karine Jean-Pierre the first Black and openly LGBTQ+ person to serve as White House press secretary
There was Lloyd Austin, the first Black man to run the Defense Department
And of course, there was Kamala Harris — the first Black and South Asian vice president and leader-of-the-Democratic-Party-in-waiting
Importantly, Black elected officials were winning outside of Washington, too
As Politico noted in 2022, the Biden years marked the first time that New York City, Houston, Chicago, and Los Angeles — America’s four most populous cities — all had elected Black mayors
But fast-forward to now, and it’s all gone a bit bleak
The John Lewis Voting Rights Act, a core Biden-Harris promise, never materialized
Harris lost to Trump in the 2024 election
And Democrats have broadly backlashed against any explicit focus on Black racial politics
Two of those mayors (Eric Adams of New York City and Lori Lightfoot of Chicago) were bounced after one term
Houston elected a white mayor, John Whitmire, who defeated Rep
Sheila Jackson Lee, a longtime member of the Congressional Black Caucus

And this November, Mayor Karen Bass of Los Angeles is at risk of becoming the latest political casualty, as she faces a tough race from an insurgent Democratic socialist, City Council member Nithya Raman
To make matters worse, the Supreme Court’s decision in Louisiana v
Callais may put as many as 19 members of the Congressional Black Caucus — nearly a third of the caucus — at risk of losing their seats, with a particular impact on the American South

And the current energy in the Democratic Party has come from its progressive left, which has found a winning formula for winning in primaries that essentially goes around Black voters — as seen in races like Zohran Mamdani’s win in New York City, or even James Talarico’s defeat of Jasmine Crockett in Texas

But here’s the point: Just a few short years after Democrats declared that “representation matters,” the Black elected officials who benefitted from that priority have largely receded into the background, and it reflects the larger crossroads facing many Black Democrats in a changing party

On one side, the choice is a failed establishment that historically made space for (some) Black causes; on the other is a progressive wing that is often working from a deficit of trust, with little history in Black communities and connection with Black political leaders.  Earlier this year, two interviews on America, Actually showed the divergent paths

The other with Angie Nixon, the Democratic nominee for the US Senate seat in Florida.  The power broker If you haven’t watched my interview with Clyburn , I’d encourage you to — because the anguish on my face is pretty palpable throughout the whole thing
It made news because of what Clyburn said (or didn’t) about artificial intelligence, but the conversation on Black politics is what most stuck with me

The Congress member explicitly blamed Black voters for Kamala Harris’s 2024 loss, saying they let her and the party down — not the other way around: Me: “So is the argument that Black people let Kamala Harris down?” Clyburn: “In many instances, absolutely…if that 59 percent had been 69 percent, she would’ve won.” He defended taking corporate dollars even as polling says most Democrats, including Black voters, wish their politicians did not

And when I asked about his two most notable endorsements since the 2024 election: supporting Andrew Cuomo against Mamdani in New York City’s mayoral race, and backing Haley Stevens against Abdul El-Sayed in the Michigan Senate race — here’s what he said: So I’m supposed to throw away all these relationships for somebody I never saw before, never heard of before…come on

Why don’t they just get off of that? At one point, I asked Clyburn whether Mamdani’s enduring popularity, including among Black New Yorkers, caused any reflection: “Oh, I’m not paying attention to that
I got 90 percent.” Clyburn didn’t just defend centrist ideology

He defended a way of politics that was fundamentally unresponsive to voters, and he plainly articulated the lack of accountability at the heart of establishment politics: We didn’t fail, the voters failed us.  But importantly, Clyburn’s policy positions — and those of the larger Congressional Black Caucus — are increasingly out of step with public opinion
Voters, including Black ones, want corporate money out of politics
And like much of the Democratic base, Black voters have also shifted left on Israel and are skeptical of things like Big Tech
Meanwhile, CBC members like Crockett are awash in crypto-industry money — from the likes of Marc Andreessen and the Winklevoss twins

At the CBC’s recent legislative conference, one of the “top sponsors” was Palantir Technologies — the data firm with major ICE contracts — even as the Congressional Hispanic Caucus canceled its financial relationship with the group

title: How October 7 changed everything
excerpt: Israelis visit the Nova music festival memorial site to mark the third anniversary of the October 7, 2023 attacks. | Saeed Qaq/Anadolu via Getty Images This sto
body: Israelis visit the Nova music festival memorial site to mark the third anniversary of the October 7, 2023 attacks. | Saeed Qaq/Anadolu via Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here
Jewish communities in Israel and around the world are currently marking the third anniversary of the October 7 attacks that killed 1,200 people and triggered the war in Gaza
Memorials for the victims of the attacks have been held at homes , on highways , and at the site of the Nova music festival
In Tel Aviv, a massive art installation at the Trumpeldor beach commemorated both the victims and the 251 hostages taken by Hamas three years ago
Of those hostages, 166 have since returned alive, and the remains of the last deceased captive were released to Israel in January
But there’s no undoing the national trauma of the October 7 attacks — the deadliest massacre of Jewish people since the Holocaust — or the brutal retaliatory campaign that Israel launched afterward
Those events profoundly changed Israel, Gaza, the broader Middle East, and the United States, and they continue to shape global and domestic politics
So today, we’re taking a look at the very long shadow of the October 7 attacks and Israel’s response to them

Go a little deeper View Link Writing about the first anniversary of October 7 two years ago, Vox’s Zack Beauchamp warned that the “horrors” first triggered by the attacks would continue to unfold in tragic and unforeseeable ways . “Events that might seem contained to the Middle East have come to hurt people around the world,” he wrote, “in ways that we may not yet fully understand or even be capable of predicting.” That hurt has undeniably been most acute in the Gaza Strip, where three years of war have reduced entire cities to rubble
Israel’s military campaign has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians — most of them civilians — since October 2023
Most of Gaza’s 2 million residents have also been displaced from their homes, crowded into makeshift shelters and refugee camps riddled with hunger and disease
But the consequences of October 7 extended beyond Gaza.  Settler violence against Palestinians intensified in the occupied West Bank
And the ensuing conflicts also weakened Iran and changed the balance of power across the Middle East
That’s because Iran had long relied on its allies, like Hamas in Gaza and Hezbollah in Lebanon, to project power and deter attacks by its longtime rival, Israel

After October 7, however, Israel  significantly weakened both groups, leaving Iran vulnerable and setting the stage for the direct strikes on Iran that Israel and the US began last winter.  Both the war in Iran and the continued occupation of Gaza have badly hurt Israel’s international image
Across 36 countries  surveyed by Pew last spring, a median of 67 percent of adults viewed Israel negatively

That disapproval has translated into diplomatic shifts, as well: 155 countries — including longtime allies of Israel, such as the United Kingdom, Canada, and Australia — now officially recognize Palestinian statehood, up from 136 before the war
That doesn’t change much on the ground , but it represents a real rebuke to Israel.  In the US, meanwhile, Israel has become a huge flashpoint in domestic politics
While more than half of Americans had a favorable view of the country before October 7, sentiment deteriorated sharply in 2025 and 2026, particularly on the left
The issue could help determine some key midterm races, like the Michigan Senate election, where Democrat Abdul El-Sayed has called for ending US military aid to Israel

That’s a policy nearly half of House Democrats and many potential presidential candidates have also endorsed .  Cutting off US aid to Israel isn’t likely to change the country’s stance toward Palestinians, however. (Israel is a wealthy country in its own right, and American aid represents just a small piece of its budget.) Instead, changing Israeli policy on Gaza and the West Bank would likely require far more aggressive pressure — pressure that, even in the current political environment, the US is unlikely to apply
A single day may have kicked off a cascade of hurt and horrors
But putting an end to them will take far more time
It can feel difficult (not to mention: naive, pointless, and exhausting) to maintain optimism in the face of current events

So Jamil Zaki, a psychology professor and the director of the Stanford Social Neuroscience Lab, suggests another tact: Do away with blind optimism and lean into hope — that belief that the future could turn out well, but requires real care and attention

Before you go… Did you know… that sea turtles regularly cry (okay: “shed tears”) to rid their bodies of excess salt? Scientists are studying sea turtle tears to learn more about animal navigation.  Today’s trivia: What’s the word for a baby eagle? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword
Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Yesterday we asked you for the final letter of the Greek alphabet
That would be omega, as in the Bible verse, Swiss watch brand, and nutritional supplement .

body: Health minister says 28 contacts identified after death of citizen who arrived from DRC on Saturday Kenya has reported its first-ever Ebola death, the health minister announced on Tuesday, as the disease continues to spread rapidly through the north-east of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where the outbreak was announced in May
This is the 17th outbreak of the highly infectious, often deadly disease in the DRC

As of 2 October, 4,082 people had died out of 8,463 confirmed cases in the country since the emergence of the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus, for which there is still no vaccine nor specific treatment

title: Guardian readers fund life-changing surgery for Somali boy injured in US airstrike

body: After Guardian investigation uncovered drone strike that killed 12 civilians and injured many more, seven-year-old Abdiqadir Salah underwent vital operation in Mogadishu On the rickshaw ride to the hospital, Marian Haji Abdi Guled felt a mixture of joy and apprehension: the day they had been waiting for had finally arrived

Almost a year earlier, her then seven-year-old son, Abdiqadir Salah, had been seriously injured, alongside his two siblings, in what a Guardian investigation found was a US drone strike on the village of Jamaame in Somalia that killed at least 12 civilians, including eight children
